title: Trie (prefix tree)
summary: A trie (prefix tree) stores strings by their prefixes. Each node represents a prefix; edges are labeled with characters. Root = empty string. A path from root to node spells the key. Used for autocomplete, spell checking, IP routing (longest prefix match), and dictionary storage. Variants: radix tree (compressed trie, merges single-child chains), Patricia trie (binary radix tree), suffix tree (all suffixes of a string).

structure.meaning: Array of child pointers (one per alphabet symbol) + terminal flag (is this a complete word?).
Each edge is labeled with a character.
Path from root to node spells the key.
Marks the end of a complete word.
Compressed trie: merges chains of single-child nodes into a single edge with a string label.
Binary radix tree: each node has 2 children (0/1). Used for IP routing (longest prefix match).
Trie of all suffixes of a string. O(n) construction (Ukkonen's algorithm). Used for string matching.
Each node has 3 children: less, equal, greater. More space-efficient than standard trie.

notes: Tries provide O(k) search where k = key length (independent of number of keys).
Tries are used in autocomplete, spell checkers, IP routing (longest prefix match), and DNS.
Radix trees (compressed tries) are used in the Linux kernel (idr, xarray) and IP routing.
Suffix trees enable O(n) string matching (after O(n) preprocessing).
Tries use more memory than hash tables (pointers per node).
